name: Nikhil Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher at the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and this conversation is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a grader at a big open-pit nickel mine, it's the machine with the long blade under the middle that keeps the haul roads smooth. Sounds boring, but if the roads are rough the truck tyres wear out, and each tyre costs more than my car, so the bosses care a lot. I'm about a year and a half in, still getting the crown on the road right, that's the slight hump so water runs off. Twelve-hour shifts, four on, four off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's tough?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the four off, honestly. I fly my drone, I mess around with AI apps, I'm teaching myself a bit of coding with one of them as my tutor. The tough part is that I'm junior on junior pay, and I send some money home every month to my dad, who wrecked his back at the factory. So I'm living alone in a small rented unit with a gaming chair and not much else, and my savings are basically zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, 'okay, the robots were oversold, back to grading.' Online I'd probably post a meme about it in the drone forum I'm on. Nobody at work would care much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit let down. I like this stuff. But it's fine for my wallet, the job stays, and I can keep learning on my own time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep grading, get better at the crown. Keep the coding hobby going, maybe finish the beginner course. Probably try to start saving, though I say that every month and then my dad's physio bill comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you using the coding for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, a little program that logs my drone flights and makes maps. It's rubbish, but it works. The AI app writes half of it and I fix the half it gets wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your bosses ever see that as useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. The survey team uses drones to measure the stockpiles. I showed one of them my map and he said 'not bad for a grader driver,' which I'm choosing to take as a compliment.

S0.say: I'd say the robots were oversold and it's back to grading. I'd post a meme in my drone forum, but nobody at work would care much.
S0.think: I think I'd be a bit let down because I like this technology. But it's fine for my wallet, the job stays and I can keep learning in my own time.
S0.do: Keeps grading and works on getting the road crown right. Continues his beginner coding course with an AI tutor and tries to start saving, though money he sends his father usually stops that.
S0.quote: The AI app writes half of it and I fix the half it gets wrong.
S0.fieldNote: He's genuinely curious about technology and treats the quiet picture as a mild letdown. The money he sends his injured father is a fixed cost that keeps his savings at zero. His drone mapping hobby already overlaps with the mine's survey work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance as much as a threat, if you're willing to learn. I'd probably say that and annoy half my crew. Online I'd share stuff about what new jobs are actually appearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think graders are pretty easy to automate, honestly. A grader on a haul road is a fixed route with sensors, and some sites already run them remotely. So my seat's going. But I'm the kind of person who could be on the other side of it, running the system or mapping the roads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a transfer to the survey team or the remote operations centre the first chance I got. I'd do a drone pilot licence, the proper commercial one, out of my own pay over a few months. And I'd start a small weekend thing doing drone photos for local farms and real estate, for extra cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, mostly. A little nervous about the money side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd annoy half your crew. Who would it annoy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mick, mostly. He's been on graders for twenty years and he thinks any talk of change is me showing off. I get it. If I were him I'd be scared too, and the scared comes out as grumpy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A commercial drone licence costs money. Where would that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the gaming PC. It's the only thing I own worth anything. I'd miss it for a week and then I'd be flying drones for money instead of playing games about it.

S1.say: I'd say it's a chance as much as a threat if you're willing to learn, which would annoy half my crew. Online I'd share what new jobs are actually appearing.
S1.think: I think graders are easy to automate because a haul road is a fixed route with sensors. My seat is going, but I could be on the other side, running the system or mapping the roads.
S1.do: Asks for a transfer to the survey team or the remote operations centre and pays for a commercial drone pilot licence by selling his gaming PC. Starts a weekend drone photography business for farms and real estate.
S1.feel: Mostly good, a little nervous about money.
S1.quote: I'd be flying drones for money instead of playing games about it.
S1.fieldNote: He's quick to accept his own seat will go and moves straight to the next role. He's ready to sell his one valuable possession to pay for training. He reads an older colleague's grumpiness as fear, which shows some empathy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt fast, and also that the government has to make sure people aren't left with nothing. I'm not usually the 'government should do it' guy, but two years is too fast for anyone to sort themselves out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even for me, two years is scary. My whole plan is to be the human who runs the machines, and in this picture the machines run themselves. I'd have a drone licence and some bad code and no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on whatever's still growing, probably the companies building and installing these robots, because for a while they'd need people on the ground. I'd move to the city for it in the first few months, even with no savings, maybe crash at my cousin's. I'd keep sending Dad money as long as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited for about five minutes, then anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen with your dad if you couldn't send money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part I don't like thinking about. My sister would have to cover more, and she's got two kids. I'd probably call her before I called anyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said excited for five minutes. What's exciting about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it would be the biggest thing to happen in my life, and I'd see it up close. I'm not going to pretend I wouldn't be curious. Curious doesn't pay rent though.

S2.say: I'd say adapt fast, and also that government has to make sure people aren't left with nothing. I'm not usually that guy, but two years is too fast for anyone to sort themselves out.
S2.think: I think even my plan of being the human who runs the machines fails if the machines run themselves. I'd have a drone licence, some bad code and no savings.
S2.do: Chases work with the companies installing robots, moving to the city in the first few months and staying with a cousin. Keeps sending his father money for as long as he can and leans on his sister if he can't.
S2.feel: Excited for a few minutes, then anxious.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture breaks the logic of his plan, and he sees that right away. He's comfortable with risk and would move with nothing saved. His real worry is his father's care falling onto his sister.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if you start now, so start now. I'd be the annoying guy at lunch telling everyone to get a second skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is decent for me. I can get into remote ops or the robot install side, build some savings, and be thirty-two with real experience. I don't know what happens after 2031, but I'd be in a better spot than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First six months: drone licence, transfer request, keep the coding going every day with the AI tutor. Year one: apply to the companies doing mine automation, even in junior roles. And I'd try to save one month of expenses, which would be a first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's the good kind of pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be in a better spot than most. Does that bother you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Mick and the older guys would have it worse, and so would anyone who hates screens. Being okay while the crew isn't, that's not a great feeling. I'd try to drag a couple of them along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm going to be the one who builds the robots, not the one they replace. He'd say 'just don't hurt your back,' because that's what he says about everything.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough if you start now, so start now. I'd be the one at lunch telling everyone to get a second skill.
S3.think: I think five years is decent for me, because I could get into remote operations or robot installation and save a bit. I don't know what happens after 2031, but I'd be in a better spot than most.
S3.do: Gets the drone licence, requests a transfer and studies coding daily with an AI tutor in the first six months. Applies to mine automation companies within a year and tries to save a month of expenses for the first time.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but he calls it the good kind of pressure.
S3.quote: I'm going to be the one who builds the robots, not the one they replace.
S3.fieldNote: He sees five years as a workable runway and lays out a fast sequence. He's uncomfortable being better off than his crew and would try to bring some along. The exchange about his dad's back was touching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so don't waste it. I'd be pushing people at work to use the time, and I'd say the company should pay for courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I think I'm fine. I'd be thirty-seven, I'd have had time to get a technical diploma and some real jobs in automation. The worry is less about me and more about whether my town still exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the same plan, but I'd do the two-year technical diploma properly instead of grabbing short courses. Keep the drone business going on weekends. Maybe stay in town longer, because I actually like it here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Weirdly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you worry whether the town still exists. What would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The petrol station coffee at four in the morning. The sports field with the dust blowing across it. And people knowing your name. You don't get that in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if the town didn't make it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone a bit. The company for not planning, the government for not caring about small places, and people like me for leaving. I don't think there's one bad guy. Just a lot of people looking after themselves.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and nobody should waste it. I'd push people at work to use the time and say the company should pay for courses.
S4.think: I think I'd be fine at thirty-seven with a diploma and real automation experience. My worry is less about me and more about whether my town still exists.
S4.do: Follows the same plan more steadily, taking a full two-year technical diploma rather than short courses. Keeps the weekend drone business running and stays in town longer because he likes it.
S4.quote: I don't think there's one bad guy. Just a lot of people looking after themselves.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he relaxes and his concern shifts from himself to his town. He spreads blame widely, including onto people like himself who leave. He'd choose a longer, proper qualification over quick courses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Everything I'm doing assumes there's a gap between the robots arriving and the robots not needing people, and in that one the gap closes. What would help is cheap or free technical courses you can do online around shifts, and some kind of support for people like my dad who can't retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask if I'd want a robot to do my job. Some days, yes. Grading the same road at three in the morning in the rain, I'd happily hand that over. I just want to still get paid.

headlineQuote: Grading the same road at three in the morning in the rain, I'd happily hand that over. I just want to still get paid.
portrait: Nikhil Kowalski is a 27-year-old junior grader operator who keeps the haul roads smooth at a large nickel mine, lives alone and sends part of his low pay to his injured father. He's curious and comfortable with risk, uses AI tools every day to learn coding and map his drone flights, and expects his own seat to be automated early. In most pictures he moves quickly towards drones, remote operations and automation work, even selling his gaming PC for a licence. The two-year picture worries him because it closes the gap his whole plan depends on, while ten years leaves him hopeful and more concerned about his town.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because it closes the gap between robots arriving and robots no longer needing people that his whole plan relies on.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap or free online technical courses he can do around shifts, and support for people like his father who can't retrain.
